title: Elite's galaxies in a tiny memory
hook: Eight galaxies, 2,048 planets in all, fit in a computer with 32 kilobytes of memory.
peek: Elite, the 1984 space trading game, let players fly between 2,048 star systems on a BBC Micro. There was no room to store them. Instead the game rebuilt every planet, the same each time, from a handful of starting numbers.
lede: David Braben and Ian Bell wrote Elite as students, releasing it in 1984 for the BBC Micro, a computer with 32 kilobytes of memory, much of it taken by the screen. Their game had eight galaxies of 256 planets each, every one with a name, economy and description. None of it was stored. A short sequence of numbers generated it all, identically for every player.

bullets.text: The game began with a few fixed numbers and repeatedly scrambled them using a simple recipe related to the Fibonacci sequence. Each step produced the next planet's position, government, tech level and name, so the same galaxy appeared every time.
Planet names such as Lave, Leesti and Diso were stitched together from a short table of two-letter chunks. The method produced names that felt alien but could still be said aloud.

The method could have produced vastly more galaxies, by some accounts trillions. The publisher, Acornsoft, pushed for a smaller universe, reportedly so the trick behind it would not show, and Braben and Bell kept just eight, a number that still let each one feel explorable.
Elite also drew its ships as wireframe 3D shapes with hidden lines removed, which was rare on home computers then. Together with the galaxy trick, it made a huge universe from very little.
